claim: Humans vary greatly in their motor learning abilities.
source: Humans vary greatly in their motor learning abilities, yet little is known about the neural mechanisms that underlie this variability.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that sets up the research question.

claim: Little is known about the neural mechanisms that underlie variability in motor learning abilities.
source: Humans vary greatly in their motor learning abilities, yet little is known about the neural mechanisms that underlie this variability.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in current knowledge.

claim: Large-scale neural dynamics inhabit a low-dimensional subspace or manifold.
source: Recent neuroimaging and electrophysiological studies demonstrate that large-scale neural dynamics inhabit a low-dimensional subspace or manifold, and that learning is constrained by this intrinsic manifold architecture.
evidence: This claim references recent neuroimaging and electrophysiological studies as support.

claim: Learning is constrained by intrinsic manifold architecture.
source: Recent neuroimaging and electrophysiological studies demonstrate that large-scale neural dynamics inhabit a low-dimensional subspace or manifold, and that learning is constrained by this intrinsic manifold architecture.
evidence: This claim is supported by references to recent studies.

claim: The overall neural excursion from manifold activity in both cognitive and sensorimotor brain networks is associated with differences in subjects' patterns of learning and relearning across days.
source: We find that the overall neural excursion from manifold activity in both cognitive and sensorimotor brain networks is associated with differences in subjects' patterns of learning and relearning across days.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on fMRI data analysis.

claim: Off-manifold activity provides an index of the relative engagement of different neural systems during learning.
source: These findings suggest that off-manifold activity provides an index of the relative engagement of different neural systems during learning, and that subject differences in patterns of learning and relearning are related to reconfiguration processes occurring in cognitive and sensorimotor networks.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: Subject differences in patterns of learning and relearning are related to reconfiguration processes occurring in cognitive and sensorimotor networks.
source: These findings suggest that off-manifold activity provides an index of the relative engagement of different neural systems during learning, and that subject differences in patterns of learning and relearning are related to reconfiguration processes occurring in cognitive and sensorimotor networks.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: Sensorimotor adaptation relies partly on implicit learning processes driven by sensory prediction errors.
source: This sensorimotor adaptation is known to rely partly on implicit learning processes, driven by sensory prediction errors reflecting the difference between the expected and sensed consequences of movement (Wolpert et al., 1995; Wolpert and Ghahramani, 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Explicit (declarative) learning processes, such as cognitive strategies, help guide behavioral adjustments during sensorimotor adaptation.
source: In addition, there is evidence that explicit (declarative) learning processes, such as cognitive strategies, also help guide behavioral adjustments, and that these operate synergistically with implicit processes (see Krakauer and Mazzoni, 2011; McDougle et al., 2016; Wolpert et al., 2011; Miyamoto et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Explicit and implicit learning processes operate synergistically.
source: In addition, there is evidence that explicit (declarative) learning processes, such as cognitive strategies, also help guide behavioral adjustments, and that these operate synergistically with implicit processes (see Krakauer and Mazzoni, 2011; McDougle et al., 2016; Wolpert et al., 2011; Miyamoto et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Implicit and explicit learning lead to slow and fast adaptation and de-adaptation, respectively.
source: Recent behavioral and computational work (McDougle et al., 2015) has suggested that these two processes operate on different timescales, with implicit and explicit learning leading to slow and fast adaptation and de-adaptation, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to McDougle et al., 2015.

claim: Implicit adaptation relies, in part, on sensory prediction errors computed in the cerebellum.
source: Although the neural systems supporting these two learning processes are not perfectly understood, there is considerable evidence that implicit adaptation relies, in part, on sensory prediction errors computed in the cerebellum (Izawa et al., 2012; Taylor et al., 2014), which are used to drive adaptation in frontal and parietal sensorimotor regions in the neocortex (McDougle et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Izawa et al., 2012 and Taylor et al., 2014.

claim: Sensory prediction errors computed in the cerebellum are used to drive adaptation in frontal and parietal sensorimotor regions in the neocortex.
source: Although the neural systems supporting these two learning processes are not perfectly understood, there is considerable evidence that implicit adaptation relies, in part, on sensory prediction errors computed in the cerebellum (Izawa et al., 2012; Taylor et al., 2014), which are used to drive adaptation in frontal and parietal sensorimotor regions in the neocortex (McDougle et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to McDougle et al., 2015.

claim: Explicit learning has been linked to higher-level working memory and inhibitory control processes.
source: Explicit learning, by contrast, has been linked to higher-level working memory and inhibitory control processes (Keisler and Shadmehr, 2010; Anguera et al., 2010; Christou et al., 2016; Drummond et al., 2015), and thus has been associated with a wide array of higher-order association areas across the neocortex (Anguera et al., 2007; Dayan and Cohen, 2011; Doyon et al., 2009; Hardwick et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Explicit learning has been associated with a wide array of higher-order association areas across the neocortex.
source: Explicit learning, by contrast, has been linked to higher-level working memory and inhibitory control processes (Keisler and Shadmehr, 2010; Anguera et al., 2010; Christou et al., 2016; Drummond et al., 2015), and thus has been associated with a wide array of higher-order association areas across the neocortex (Anguera et al., 2007; Dayan and Cohen, 2011; Doyon et al., 2009; Hardwick et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Explicit learning is responsible for 'savings', or faster relearning upon reexposure to the task.
source: There is also evidence that explicit learning is responsible for 'savings', or faster relearning upon reexposure to the task (Haith et al., 2015; Morehead et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Haith et al., 2015 and Morehead et al., 2015.

claim: Individual differences in rates of adaptation and savings is largely driven by subject-level differences in the contribution of explicit processes to learning.
source: Moreover, emerging behavioral evidence indicates that individual differences in rates of adaptation and savings is largely driven by subject-level differences in the contribution of explicit processes to learning (de Brouwer et al., 2018; Fernandez-Ruiz et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to de Brouwer et al., 2018 and Fernandez-Ruiz et al., 2011.

claim: Activity patterns of neurons and brain regions primarily occupy a low-dimensional subspace or manifold.
source: This architecture results in correlations between the activity of neurons (and between brain regions), resulting in patterns of activation that primarily occupy a low-dimensional subspace or manifold (Gallego et al., 2017; Sadtler et al., 2014; Shenoy et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gallego et al., 2017, Sadtler et al., 2014, and Shenoy et al., 2013.

claim: Manifold structure has been observed at the level of whole-brain functional networks via functional MRI.
source: In neurophysiological studies, this manifold structure has been observed both at the level of whole-brain functional networks (via functional MRI [fMRI]; Shine et al., 2019) and at the level of local neural populations (Sadtler et al., 2014; Gallego et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Shine et al., 2019.

claim: Manifold structure has been observed at the level of local neural populations.
source: In neurophysiological studies, this manifold structure has been observed both at the level of whole-brain functional networks (via functional MRI [fMRI]; Shine et al., 2019) and at the level of local neural populations (Sadtler et al., 2014; Gallego et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Sadtler et al., 2014 and Gallego et al., 2017.

claim: Some types of learning are associated with a reconfiguration of low-dimensional manifold structure, allowing the brain to generate new patterns of off-manifold activity.
source: Recent work has suggested that some types of learning are associated with a reconfiguration of this low-dimensional structure, allowing the brain to generate new patterns of off-manifold activity (Shine et al., 2019; Oby et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Shine et al., 2019 and Oby et al., 2019.

claim: Subjects successfully reduced their error over the course of the learning epoch.
source: Mean error curves across subjects for each day are shown in Figure 2a (top), confirming that subjects successfully reduced their error over the course of the learning epoch.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Clustering revealed three distinct subgroups of learners: subjects who exhibited fast learning on both days (FF, N = 16), slow learning on both days (SS, N = 9), and slow learning on day 1 but fast learning on day 2 (SF, N = 7).
source: This clustering revealed three distinct subgroups of learners (Figure 2b), which corresponded to subjects who exhibited fast learning on both days (FF, N = 16), slow learning on both days (SS, N = 9), and slow learning on day 1 but fast learning on day 2 (SF, N = 7; Figure 2c).
evidence: This claim is based on clustering analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 2b and 2c.

claim: A three cluster solution best explained the behavioral data.
source: Based on these simulations, we judged that a three cluster solution best explained the data (Figure 2b, bottom).
evidence: This claim is based on statistical evaluation comparing cluster solutions to a null model.

claim: The rapid adaptation and de-adaptation shown by the FF group on both days, and by the SF group on day 2, are considered signatures of explicit learning.
source: The rapid adaptation and de-adaptation shown by the FF group on both days, and by the SF group on day 2, are considered signatures of explicit learning (Benson et al., 2011; de Brouwer et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Benson et al., 2011 and de Brouwer et al., 2018.

claim: The FF and SF groups show comparable performance during late learning and washout on day 1.
source: This second possibility is supported by similarity between the FF and SF groups later on day 1 (Figure 2d): both groups show comparable performance during late learning and washout (Figure 2c).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 2c and 2d.

claim: The FF and SF groups display relatively long reaction times compared to the SS group.
source: The FF and SF groups also display relatively long reaction times compared to the SS group (Figure 2d), which have been associated with explicit strategy use (e.g., Fernandez-Ruiz et al., 2011; Haith et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 2d and citations to prior work.

claim: Long reaction times have been associated with explicit strategy use.
source: The FF and SF groups also display relatively long reaction times compared to the SS group (Figure 2d), which have been associated with explicit strategy use (e.g., Fernandez-Ruiz et al., 2011; Haith et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Fernandez-Ruiz et al., 2011 and Haith et al., 2015.

claim: A sharp peak in excursion in the cognitive network was observed immediately after the onset of rotation, most pronounced on day 1, but also prominent on day 2.
source: Figure 3a shows the mean excursion across subjects in the cognitive and sensorimotor networks on each day. Notably, we observed a sharp peak in excursion in the cognitive network immediately after the onset of rotation, which is most pronounced on day 1, but also prominent on day 2.
evidence: This claim is based on excursion data shown in Figure 3a.

claim: The FF and SF groups show greater peak magnitude in the cognitive network on day 1 compared to SS.
source: Figure 3b shows the post-rotation peak broken down by behavioral group, revealing what appears to be greater peak magnitude in the FF and SF groups (compared to SS) in the cognitive network on day 1, and a greater peak in the SF group on day 2, where these subjects succeed in reducing their early error in a similar fashion to FF subjects.
evidence: This claim is based on data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: The SF group shows a greater peak in cognitive network excursion on day 2.
source: Figure 3b shows the post-rotation peak broken down by behavioral group, revealing what appears to be greater peak magnitude in the FF and SF groups (compared to SS) in the cognitive network on day 1, and a greater peak in the SF group on day 2, where these subjects succeed in reducing their early error in a similar fashion to FF subjects.
evidence: This claim is based on data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Three functional principal components together describe 77% of the variance across all excursion curves.
source: Based on variance explained by each component, we retained three components for analysis, which together describe 77% of the variance across all excursion curves.
evidence: This claim is based on multivariate functional PCA analysis of excursion data.

claim: For component 3, there was no significant effect of group.
source: Finally, for component 3, we found no significant effect of group.
evidence: This claim is based on statistical analysis of component scores.

claim: Both the FF and SF groups show a large degree of excursion in the cognitive network on the first day, with the SF group likewise showing a spike in excursion on day 2.
source: In summary, interpreting both the results of the mfPCA and the mean excursion shown in Figure 3a, both the FF and SF groups show a large degree of excursion in the cognitive network on the first day, with the SF group likewise showing a spike in excursion on day 2.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the mfPCA and excursion results.

claim: Subjects exhibit strong individual differences in functional connectivity.
source: Previous work (e.g., Gratton et al., 2018) has found that subjects exhibit strong individual differences in functional connectivity, which are likely to obscure learning- or task-related changes in network structure.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gratton et al., 2018.

claim: Prior to centering, network structure is completely dominated by subject-level clustering, with no hint of any task-related structure.
source: As can be seen in Figures 5b and 6b, prior to the centering, the network structure is completely dominated by subject-level clustering, with no hint of any task-related structure (i.e., separation of baseline, early, and late learning).
evidence: This claim is based on UMAP visualization shown in Figures 5b and 6b.

claim: Following the centering procedure, a clear task-related structure is apparent, particularly between the baseline epoch and the two learning epochs (early and late).
source: However, following the centering procedure, a clear task-related structure is now apparent, particularly between the baseline epoch and the two learning epochs (early and late).
evidence: This claim is based on UMAP visualization after centering.

claim: Task-related structure is present in both the cognitive and sensorimotor networks after centering.
source: Notably, this task-related structure is present in both the cognitive and sensorimotor networks.
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of centered covariance matrices.

claim: The FF and SF groups show almost identical trajectories on both days in the cognitive network embedding.
source: These scores are shown in Figure 5e, where the arrows denote the passage of time (from baseline, to early, to late learning), revealing, quite strikingly, that the FF and SF groups show almost identical trajectories on both days, distinct from the SS group.
evidence: This claim is based on component scores shown in Figure 5e.

claim: The first cognitive network component encodes a decrease in functional connectivity within the DA network, along with an increase in functional connectivity between the DA and the FP networks.
source: The first component can be seen to encode a decrease in functional connectivity within the DA network, along with an increase in functional connectivity between the DA and the FP networks.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the first component based on the embedding analysis.

claim: The expression of the second cognitive network component increases from baseline, to early, to late learning, and is expressed more strongly in the FF and SF groups than in the SS group.
source: The expression of this component increases from baseline, to early, to late learning, and is expressed more strongly in the FF and SF groups than in the SS group.
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of component scores across epochs and groups.

claim: The first sensorimotor component encodes the overall change in connectivity with the dorsal somatomotor regions, with baseline and early learning epochs showing a global decrease relative to resting state, which either disappears or reverses during late learning.
source: In Figure 6f, we see that the first component encodes the overall change in connectivity with the dorsal somatomotor regions, with baseline and early learning epochs showing a global decrease relative to resting state, which either disappears or reverses during late learning.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the first sensorimotor component based on the embedding analysis.

claim: The second sensorimotor component encodes an increase in connectivity within each of the dorsal and lateral somatomotor networks, and a decrease in connectivity between them.
source: The second sensorimotor component encodes an increase in connectivity within each of the dorsal and lateral somatomotor networks, and a decrease in connectivity between them.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the second sensorimotor component based on the embedding analysis.

claim: The SF subjects engage their cognitive systems in a different fashion from the SS subjects over the course of learning.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that, despite similarities in early learning performance between the SF and SS subjects, the SF subjects appear to engage their cognitive systems in a different fashion from the SS subjects over the course of learning.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the network embedding results.

claim: Both FF and SF groups show greater functional connectivity within and between the DA and FP networks (cognitive component 2).
source: In particular, consistent with the idea that the FF and SF recruit their cognitive systems in a similar fashion, we find that both groups show greater functional connectivity within and between the DA and FP networks (cognitive component 2).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the second cognitive network component results.

claim: Some neural activity patterns are more difficult to generate than others, and this constrains learning.
source: Prior work has shown that some neural activity patterns are more difficult to generate than others, and that this constrains learning Sadtler et al., 2014.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sadtler et al., 2014.

claim: The performance patterns exhibited by the FF group, including rapid learning, unlearning, and relearning, are consistent with the use of an explicit cognitive strategy.
source: The performance patterns exhibited by the FF group, including rapid learning, unlearning, and relearning, are consistent with the use of an explicit cognitive strategy (Leow et al., 2017; de Brouwer et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Leow et al., 2017 and de Brouwer et al., 2018.

claim: The embedding of subject cognitive networks revealed that network structure in the FF and SF groups were highly similar during learning across both days.
source: Consistent with this idea, the embedding of subject cognitive networks revealed that network structure in the FF and SF groups were highly similar during learning across both days (Figure 5e).
evidence: This claim is based on the network embedding analysis shown in Figure 5e.

claim: The FF and SF groups' cognitive networks exhibited greater excursion from intrinsic network structure during the learning phase, after onset of the VMR.
source: Our excursion analysis further revealed that these groups' cognitive networks exhibited greater excursion from intrinsic network structure during the learning phase, after onset of the VMR.
evidence: This claim is based on the excursion analysis results.

claim: Both the FF and SF groups, who display behavioral characteristics consistent with the use of explicit, cognitive strategy use, engage their cognitive brain networks in a manner that is distinct from gradual learners, and to a greater degree.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that both the FF and SF groups, who display behavioral characteristics consistent with the use of explicit, cognitive strategy use, engage their cognitive brain networks in a manner that is distinct from gradual learners, and to a greater degree.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: The DA network is implicated in the top-down orientation of spatial attention.
source: The DA network in particular is implicated in the top-down orientation of spatial attention (Simpson et al., 2011; Corbetta and Shulman, 2002), and is known to be modulated by the FP network during goal-directed cognition (Spreng et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Simpson et al., 2011 and Corbetta and Shulman, 2002.

claim: The DA network is modulated by the FP network during goal-directed cognition.
source: The DA network in particular is implicated in the top-down orientation of spatial attention (Simpson et al., 2011; Corbetta and Shulman, 2002), and is known to be modulated by the FP network during goal-directed cognition (Spreng et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Spreng et al., 2013.

claim: The increase in connectivity within and between the FP and DA networks in the FF and SF groups may reflect the deliberate reorienting of attention during task performance.
source: The increase in connectivity within and between these networks in the FF and SF groups may then reflect the deliberate reorienting of attention during task performance, which would be consistent with the finding of de Brouwer et al., 2018, that explicit learners alter their gaze behavior to reflect their intended aim direction in response to a VMR.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the network connectivity findings, supported by a citation to de Brouwer et al., 2018.

claim: Explicit learners alter their gaze behavior to reflect their intended aim direction in response to a VMR.
source: The increase in connectivity within and between these networks in the FF and SF groups may then reflect the deliberate reorienting of attention during task performance, which would be consistent with the finding of de Brouwer et al., 2018, that explicit learners alter their gaze behavior to reflect their intended aim direction in response to a VMR.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to de Brouwer et al., 2018.

claim: The DA network has been implicated in motor inhibition.
source: The DA network has also been implicated in motor inhibition (Hsu et al., 2020), which in the VMR task is thought to be essential for the initial suppression of a motor response to the actual target prior to implementation of a re-aiming strategy (Drummond et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hsu et al., 2020.

claim: In the VMR task, motor inhibition is thought to be essential for the initial suppression of a motor response to the actual target prior to implementation of a re-aiming strategy.
source: The DA network has also been implicated in motor inhibition (Hsu et al., 2020), which in the VMR task is thought to be essential for the initial suppression of a motor response to the actual target prior to implementation of a re-aiming strategy (Drummond et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Drummond et al., 2015.

claim: The reduced connectivity in the DA network in the SS compared to the FF/SF groups might reflect weaker engagement of the motor inhibition system.
source: The reduced connectivity in the DA network in the SS compared to the FF/SF groups might then reflect weaker engagement of this system.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the network connectivity findings.

claim: Weaker engagement of motor inhibition in SS learners would be consistent with their shorter response times, as initial inhibition and successful deployment of a re-aiming strategy are believed to require longer preparation.
source: This would also be consistent with the shorter response times in SS, as this initial inhibition and the successful deployment of a re-aiming strategy are believed to require longer preparation (Fernandez-Ruiz et al., 2011).
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by a citation to Fernandez-Ruiz et al., 2011.

claim: Initial inhibition and successful deployment of a re-aiming strategy are believed to require longer preparation.
source: This would also be consistent with the shorter response times in SS, as this initial inhibition and the successful deployment of a re-aiming strategy are believed to require longer preparation (Fernandez-Ruiz et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Fernandez-Ruiz et al., 2011.

claim: Subcortical and cerebellar regions loaded relatively weakly on the components extracted in both the cognitive and sensorimotor networks.
source: It is notable that subcortical and cerebellar regions loaded relatively weakly on the components extracted in both the cognitive and sensorimotor networks.
evidence: This is an observation from the network embedding analysis.

claim: The cerebellum plays a key role in sensorimotor adaptation.
source: This, however, should not be taken to suggest that these regions are not functionally engaged during learning, as the cerebellum in particular is known to play a key role in sensorimotor adaptation.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge.

claim: Low-dimensional structure in the activity of local neural populations is generally believed to result from the underlying network organization.
source: Low-dimensional structure in the activity of local neural populations is generally believed to result from the underlying network organization, with structural connections imposing strong constraints on the activity patterns expressible by the network.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge in the field.

claim: Structural connections impose strong constraints on the activity patterns expressible by neural networks.
source: Low-dimensional structure in the activity of local neural populations is generally believed to result from the underlying network organization, with structural connections imposing strong constraints on the activity patterns expressible by the network.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge in the field.

claim: Behaviors requiring the generation of on-manifold activity are learned more quickly than behaviors requiring novel, off-manifold activation.
source: Several authors, such as Sadtler et al., 2014, have suggested that this structure may, in turn, impose constraints on learning, such that behaviors requiring the generation of on-manifold activity are learned more quickly than behaviors requiring novel, off-manifold activation.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sadtler et al., 2014.

claim: Whole-brain fMRI BOLD activity displays low-dimensional structure.
source: Although whole-brain fMRI BOLD activity is likewise known to display low-dimensional structure (e.g., Gao et al., 2020), its origins are likely to involve not only the underlying structural connectivity, but also shared function, shared sensory input, and correlations introduced by shared activation during cognitive tasks.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gao et al., 2020.

claim: The origins of low-dimensional structure in whole-brain fMRI BOLD activity likely involve not only underlying structural connectivity, but also shared function, shared sensory input, and correlations introduced by shared activation during cognitive tasks.
source: Although whole-brain fMRI BOLD activity is likewise known to display low-dimensional structure (e.g., Gao et al., 2020), its origins are likely to involve not only the underlying structural connectivity, but also shared function, shared sensory input, and correlations introduced by shared activation during cognitive tasks.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the nature of low-dimensional structure in fMRI data.

claim: In the context of large-scale brain networks, excursion from resting manifold structure is likely to reflect, at least partly, a change in the functional organization of these networks.
source: In the context of large-scale brain networks, then, excursion from resting manifold structure is likely to reflect, at least partly, a change in the functional organization of these networks.
evidence: This is an interpretation of what excursion measures in the context of fMRI.

claim: The spike in excursion after rotation onset was most prominent in the FF and SF groups.
source: We observed a large spike in excursion after rotation onset, located predominantly in the cognitive networks, and which was largest on the first day. This spike was most prominent in the FF and SF groups, which show behavioral traits consistent with explicit learning.
evidence: This is based on the excursion analysis results.

claim: The excursion spike does not appear to be a response to error, as the SS group showed less cognitive excursion than both the FF and SF groups, despite greater errors on both days.
source: The excursion does not appear to be a response to error, as the SS group showed less cognitive excursion than both the FF and SF groups, despite greater errors on both days.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on comparing excursion patterns with error patterns across groups.

claim: The excursion spike does not appear to reflect the pure recall of a strategy itself, as the spike was dampened in the FF group on the second day, while being maintained in the SF group.
source: Nor does it appear to reflect the pure recall of a strategy itself, as the spike was dampened in the FF group on the second day, while being maintained in the SF group.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on comparing excursion patterns across days and groups.

claim: The excursion may reflect cognitive network engagement involved in the learning or refinement of an explicit strategy, and not in the recall or implementation of the strategy itself.
source: This may suggest that the excursion reflects cognitive network engagement involved in the learning or refinement of an explicit strategy, and not in the recall or implementation of the strategy itself.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the excursion findings.

claim: Sensorimotor regions receive substantial top-down modulation from higher-order cognitive regions.
source: In truth, sensorimotor regions receive substantial top-down modulation from higher-order cognitive regions, and these connections are likely essential for successful learning and performance (Mars et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Mars et al., 2011.

claim: Connections between sensorimotor and higher-order cognitive regions are likely essential for successful learning and performance.
source: In truth, sensorimotor regions receive substantial top-down modulation from higher-order cognitive regions, and these connections are likely essential for successful learning and performance (Mars et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Mars et al., 2011.

claim: The functional PCA of subject excursion revealed higher excursion in sensorimotor as well as cognitive networks in FF and SF learners.
source: It is worth noting that our fPCA (Figure 4b) of subject excursion revealed higher excursion in sensorimotor as well as cognitive networks in FF and SF learners, which suggests a functional reconfiguration of sensorimotor network structure in explicit learners.
evidence: This claim is based on the fPCA results shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Higher excursion in sensorimotor networks in FF and SF learners suggests a functional reconfiguration of sensorimotor network structure in explicit learners.
source: It is worth noting that our fPCA (Figure 4b) of subject excursion revealed higher excursion in sensorimotor as well as cognitive networks in FF and SF learners, which suggests a functional reconfiguration of sensorimotor network structure in explicit learners.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the fPCA results.

claim: Functional reconfiguration of sensorimotor networks may be partly a consequence of a change in cognitive networks, and a resulting change in the functional connections between cognitive and sensorimotor regions.
source: This may itself be partly a consequence of a change in cognitive networks, and a resulting change in the functional connections between cognitive and sensorimotor regions.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the relationship between cognitive and sensorimotor network changes.

claim: Report trials can alter subject performance on the VMR task and magnify the use of explicit strategies.
source: However, there is considerable evidence (e.g., Leow et al., 2017; de Brouwer et al., 2018) that these trials can alter subject performance on the task and magnify the use of these strategies.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Leow et al., 2017 and de Brouwer et al., 2018.

claim: Subject reports strongly correlate with measures of error and other assays of explicit learning.
source: Nevertheless, subject reports strongly correlate both with our measures of error and other assays of explicit learning (Leow et al., 2017; de Brouwer et al., 2018), and measures such as savings and learning rate are linked to explicit learning processes by a large literature, both behavioral and computational (e.g., McDougle et al., 2015; Morehead et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Leow et al., 2017 and de Brouwer et al., 2018.

claim: Measures such as savings and learning rate are linked to explicit learning processes.
source: Nevertheless, subject reports strongly correlate both with our measures of error and other assays of explicit learning (Leow et al., 2017; de Brouwer et al., 2018), and measures such as savings and learning rate are linked to explicit learning processes by a large literature, both behavioral and computational (e.g., McDougle et al., 2015; Morehead et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to McDougle et al., 2015 and Morehead et al., 2015.

claim: Forty right-handed individuals between the ages of 18 and 35 (M = 22.5, SD = 4.51; 13 males) participated in the study.
source: Forty right-handed individuals between the ages of 18 and 35 (M = 22.5, SD = 4.51; 13 males) participated in the study and received financial compensation for their time.
evidence: This is a description of the study participants.

claim: Participants performed hand movements directed toward a target by applying a directional force onto an MRI-compatible force sensor using their right index finger and thumb.
source: Participants performed hand movements directed toward a target by applying a directional force onto an MRI-compatible force sensor (ATI technologies) using their right index finger and thumb.
evidence: This describes the experimental apparatus and procedure.

claim: During each testing session, 120 baseline trials (15 sets of eight trials) were completed without a rotation of the cursor.
source: During each testing session, 120 baseline trials (15 sets of eight trials) were completed without a rotation of the cursor.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: Following baseline trials, 320 learning trials (40 sets of eight trials) were completed, wherein a 45° clockwise rotation of the cursor was applied.
source: Following these trials, 320 learning trials (40 sets of eight trials) were completed, wherein a 45° clockwise rotation of the cursor was applied.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: Following the learning scan, 120 washout trials were completed in a separate scan with conditions restored to baseline (no rotation of cursor).
